message.content: Although an Leshy, Pebble Spring became immediately fascinated by the mortal settlements when they set foot in a city. They loves the nicely paved ground, the intricate bridges, and the most of all, they loved houses. The nicely layed out stone walls forming shelters from the weathers yet connect the earth with the stories from every family. They decided to learn the craft of housebuilding with the help of a touch of arcane magic from their self-made staff. The first time they stepped into the bustling marketplace, the noise and chaos filled them with a strange sense of wonder. They watched as merchants called out their wares, and the smell of fresh bread mingled with the earthy scent of the forest. The Leshy found themselves drawn to the workshops where craftsmen hammered and chiseled away at stone and wood. Every building they passed told a different tale of the people who had raised it from the ground. They marveled at how the mortals turned raw materials into something warm and inviting. A simple thatched roof could shelter an entire family from the harshest winter storms. The Leshy returned to the forest each night, still carrying the image of those sturdy walls in their mind. They sketched rough designs in the dirt with a sharpened stick, trying to replicate what they had seen. The self-made staff hummed faintly whenever they traced a line that might hold. Slowly, the arcane symbols etched into the staff began to glow with a soft amber light. The magic whispered suggestions, nudging their clumsy hands toward better angles and sturdier joints. They gathered stones from the riverbank and carried them back one by one to their clearing. Each rock was carefully placed, guided by the gentle pulse of the staff against their palm. The Leshy worked through the long autumn nights, the forest around them growing quiet with sleep. By the time the first frost crept over the meadow, the outline of a small dwelling had taken shape. It was far from perfect, with gaps where the stones did not quite meet. The roof sagged unevenly, and one wall listed to the left like a tired traveler. Yet it stood, and in that moment, something in the Leshy's ancient heart swelled with quiet pride. They had built something that the mortals would call a home, however rough it may have been. The very first house that they attempted to build with their newly learned craft of housebuilding after many long weeks of careful and very patient practice and lots of failed attempts was a rather spotty and uneven little structure that barely held together in the wind.
